Friday night
Today in the lunch break Neel said "vegetable" in his funny accent again and I just copied it, loudly. Irawati laughed so hard she choked on her juice. Then the whole table was laughing. Even Kartik, who never laughs at my jokes.
For the rest of the day people kept saying it at me. "Do the vegetable thing, Asif!" I felt like a king. Like I finally belonged at the front table, not the corner.
Neel didn't say anything. He went red and ate the rest of his lunch with his head down. I saw it. I just didn't think about it much. Tomorrow I might do the one about his shoes.
Asif

qa.a: Irawati laughed so hard she choked on her juice.

qa.q: What did Asif feel when people kept asking him to do the accent?
qa.a: He felt powerful and accepted, "like a king," as if he finally belonged at the front table.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Asif at this stage?
qa.a: He could take seriously what he saw, Neel going red and eating with his head down, and choose not to do the next joke, looking for belonging in ways that do not cost someone else.

qa.q: How is Neel experiencing the lunch table's laughter?
qa.a: He is likely humiliated and alone, going red and eating with his head down while the whole table laughs at him.

grounding: It shows a teen who wants status discovering that mocking a classmate wins the group's laughter, a reward that outweighs the target's pain for him.

subtype: Stage 1: Status and a group's approval [Actor]
passage:
I found out in Class 9 how easy it is to become popular. I'm Naveen, and this is not a proud story.

Vikas was the new boy, from a small town, with a thick accent. One day in the canteen I copied the way he said "biscuit". The whole table laughed, including Dev and Aditi, who had never even looked at me before.

The next day I did it again. More people laughed. Dev saved me a seat. I was invited to a birthday I'd never have been invited to.

I saw Vikas's face, of course. I saw him eat his lunch faster and leave. But the laughter felt so good that his face didn't seem to matter as much.

That's the part I think about now. It wasn't that I didn't see him. I saw him, and I chose the laughs.

qa.q: What word of Vikas's did Naveen copy?
qa.a: "Biscuit".

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when the table laughed?
qa.a: Naveen felt accepted and important, as the group's approval felt so good that Vikas's hurt seemed not to matter.

qa.q: What turning point was available to Naveen at this stage?
qa.a: When Naveen saw Vikas leave the canteen, Naveen could have stopped and chosen Vikas's feelings over the group's laughter.

qa.q: How did Vikas seem to feel in the canteen?
qa.a: He seemed hurt and embarrassed, eating faster and leaving.

grounding: Naveen recalls mocking a new boy's accent to win the group's laughter and approval, a reward that outweighed the target's visible hurt.

subtype: Stage 1: Status and a group's approval [Actor]
passage:
Teacher's note, Class 10B, Monday

During group work I noticed Ayesha doing an impression of Farah, who has a slight lisp. The group around her laughed loudly. Ayesha looked around at them, delighted, and did it again.

Ayesha is bright but has had a hard term; she has recently fallen out with her old friends. Today, for the first time in weeks, a popular group was laughing with her. I could see how much that meant to her. I could also see Farah staring at her notebook, ears red.

I stopped the activity and spoke to the class about respect, without naming anyone. After class I spoke privately to Ayesha: I was clear that mocking Farah must stop, and I asked how she was doing. She cried a little and said she felt invisible lately.

I have informed the counsellor about both girls, and I checked on Farah before she went home.

— Pallavi Ma'am

qa.q: What did Ayesha imitate?
qa.a: Farah's slight lisp.

qa.q: Why did the laughter matter so much to Ayesha?
qa.a: After falling out with her old friends she felt invisible, so the group's approval felt powerful and made her feel wanted.

qa.q: Which of Pallavi Ma'am's choices were wise, and why?
qa.a: She stopped the mockery without naming anyone, was clear with Ayesha privately while asking how she was, checked on Farah and told the counsellor.

qa.q: How was Farah feeling during the impression?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, staring at her notebook with red ears.

grounding: A teacher's note shows Ayesha discovering that mocking a classmate wins a group's laughter, an approval that outweighs the target's pain, and the teacher's response.

Monday, 10 p.m.
Today in bio, Sharmila answered a question with her usual long, careful speech, and I did her voice under my breath: "Excuse me, ma'am, technically..." Aditi snorted. Then Kiran, then the whole back row. Even Zara from the top table turned round and grinned at me. That grin. I've wanted that table to notice me since Class 8.
At lunch they saved me a seat. Someone said, "Noor, do the Sharmila voice again," so I did, and they laughed even harder. Sharmila was two tables away. I saw her put her sandwich down and stop eating. I felt a tiny pinch. But mostly I felt like I had finally got in.
I'll probably do it again tomorrow. Is that bad? It doesn't feel bad while they're laughing.

qa.a: Noor did Sharmila's voice under the breath: "Excuse me, ma'am, technically..."

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when the top table saved a seat at lunch?
qa.a: Noor felt thrilled and accepted, as if finally let in, and that approval outweighed the tiny pinch of guilt.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Noor before tomorrow?
qa.a: Noor could take that pinch seriously, remember Sharmila putting the sandwich down, and look for ways to belong that don't cost someone else.

qa.q: What is Sharmila experiencing two tables away?
qa.a: Sharmila seems hurt and humiliated, putting her sandwich down and not eating while the table laughs at her voice.
